scenes.narration: You decide to skip sleep for three days. Not forever. Just seventy-two hours. By the end, your brain will be doing things you won't notice until they cost you something.

props.title: What if you stayed awake for 72 hours?
props.subtitle: Hour by hour

scenes.narration: The first sixteen hours feel normal. You are just a person who is awake. Meanwhile a chemical called adenosine builds up in your brain, and that is the pressure to sleep.
Around hour twenty-four, things change. Studies on sleep loss find that a full day awake can slow your reactions about as much as being over the legal drink-drive limit.
The pattern is a chain. Less sleep means slower attention. Slower attention means you miss details. Missing details means mistakes, and you are the last person to notice them.

Then come microsleeps. Your brain drops out for a few seconds at a time, even with your eyes open. You might read a sentence and have no memory of it. Behind a wheel, those seconds are the dangerous part.
Here is the trick. What you feel and what your brain is doing drift apart. You feel fine, just a bit tired. Your brain is skipping seconds and judging risk badly.
By hour seventy-two, many people report seeing or hearing things that are not there. Moods swing. Simple tasks feel enormous, and your sense of time stretches and warps.
And then, finally, you sleep. Your brain does not repay every lost hour. It collects the deepest sleep first, and often a couple of long nights is enough to feel like yourself again.
So the honest answer is this. Three days awake will not break you, but it will quietly change how you think, long before you feel it.

props.title: Sleep is not optional
props.subtitle: Your brain notices before you do
